prompt: A colleague proposes generating codes by taking the first 7 base62 characters of `SHA-256(longUrl)`. The service will hold hundreds of billions of links. What is the main problem?

options.text: SHA-256 is too slow to compute at 3,000 writes per second.
options.explanation: Wrong. No hardware benchmark is supplied; the demonstrated problem is namespace collisions, not an established hashing bottleneck.

options.text: Hash-based codes can't be stored in a key-value store.
options.explanation: Wrong. A hash-derived code is just a string key; any KV store handles it. The issue is uniqueness, not storage.

options.text: Distinct inputs can map to the same short code, requiring atomic code collision detection and retries; identical input URLs also share a code unless ownership is included.
options.explanation: Correct. Finite truncated outputs are not unique identifiers by themselves. Both code collisions and the intended ownership semantics need an explicit policy.

options.text: Hashes are reversible, so attackers can recover the long URL from the code.
options.explanation: Wrong. Cryptographic hashes are designed to make finding an input for a specified output computationally difficult. A truncated code loses information and cannot uniquely identify its original URL; finding a matching guessed input is a different task and a shorter output can make matching easier. Predictable input URLs can still be guessed and hashed, and a densely occupied short namespace can be probed.

workedExample: A hash produces a candidate code, not proof of uniqueness. Truncation puts many possible URLs into a finite namespace, so distinct inputs can collide even well before it is full. Use an atomic insert-if-absent and retry with another candidate; a separate existence check races with other writers. Including an owner identifier separates ownership but changes deduplication semantics.
